platforms.title: Dawn Phenomenon vs. Somogyi Effect: Morning Blood Sugar
platforms.meta_description: Waking up with higher blood sugar than at bedtime doesn't always mean an error. How to tell the dawn phenomenon apart from the Somogyi effect.
platforms.body_html:
Ate nothing overnight, but your morning blood sugar reads higher than it did at bedtime? The American Diabetes Association explains that this pattern can be a normal hormonal response called the dawn phenomenon. But the exact same result can also come from a completely different cause, the Somogyi effect, and telling them apart matters.

Why blood sugar rises without eating anything at all

Between roughly 3 a.m. and 8 a.m., the body releases hormones like growth hormone, cortisol, and glucagon as part of getting ready to wake up. These hormones signal the liver to release stored glucose into the bloodstream, prewarming the body with energy for the day ahead. When insulin is working normally, it buffers that rise, but with insulin resistance, prediabetes, or diabetes, the increase becomes noticeable enough to show up as a clearly higher fasting reading in the morning.

The Somogyi effect looks similar but comes from a different cause entirely: blood sugar drops too low overnight, and the body overcorrects by releasing stress hormones, rebounding to a high reading by morning. It usually happens when diabetes medication or insulin timing and dosing aren't quite matched to the body's needs.

How to tell them apart, and what to be careful about

First, checking blood sugar around 2 to 3 a.m. for a few nights. If it stays steady or climbs gradually through the night rather than dropping, that points to the dawn phenomenon. If it dips low around that time and then rebounds high by morning, that points to the Somogyi effect.

Second, whether night sweats, nightmares, or a morning headache show up alongside it. Those symptoms suggest a low blood sugar episode happened overnight, which lines up with the Somogyi effect.

What matters most is not adjusting evening medication or insulin dosing on your own without confirming which pattern it is. The dawn phenomenon may call for adjusting the timing or dose of morning medication, but the Somogyi effect actually needs a lower evening dose — the fixes point in opposite directions. Getting it wrong can make overnight low blood sugar worse, so any dosing change is worth deciding together with a doctor.

Waking up at 2 or 3 a.m. every night just to test isn't realistic for most people, which is one reason a continuous glucose monitor can be worth asking a doctor about — it tracks the overnight curve automatically and shows exactly whether the line dips before it rises or just climbs steadily the whole time. Even without one, jotting down a few nights of readings alongside what was eaten and when medication was taken gives a doctor a much clearer picture than a single morning number on its own, since the same fasting reading can mean two very different things depending on what happened a few hours earlier.

The takeaway: a higher fasting reading in the morning doesn't automatically mean something went wrong. Check blood sugar around 2 to 3 a.m. to pin down the actual cause, and always loop in a doctor before changing any medication dose.
